etymology: From Old French vois, from Latin vox. The Hebrew qōl is broader than the English and this breadth matters: it means any sound — thunder, a trumpet, the noise of a crowd, the rustle of leaves — as well as the speech of a person. The King James translators keep the width, which is why Adam heard the voice of the LORD God walking in the garden, and why the same word can render the roar of many waters. In Scripture a voice is not merely a sound but a sound with someone behind it.
biblical_def: Voice in Scripture is the mark of a personal God who speaks, and the response a man makes to it is the measure of his standing. Religion begins in Genesis not with a vision but with a sound, and the sound drives the guilty into hiding: “And they heard the voice of the LORD God walking in the garden in the cool of the day: and Adam and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God amongst the trees of the garden” (Gen 3:8). The voice that had made the world and called it good is now the voice a sinner runs from. That voice is neither weak nor tame: “The voice of the LORD is powerful; the voice of the LORD is full of majesty” (Psa 29:4). Yet God's characteristic way of dealing with a discouraged servant is not by force. Elijah, having demanded fire, is taught the lesson at Horeb: the wind, the earthquake, and the fire pass, “and after the fire a still small voice” (1Ki 19:12) — the LORD being in the whisper rather than the spectacle. The New Testament resolves the whole matter into a question of recognition. Sheep do not analyse the shepherd's voice; they know it: “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me” (Joh 10:27). Hearing here is not the physical act, since many heard Christ and went away; it is the effectual hearing of those given to Him. The final summons will be by voice also, and the dead will not be able to hide from it as Adam did among the trees.
webster_summary: Sound uttered by the mouth; the faculty of speech; and in Scripture the voice of the LORD in the garden, in the thunder, in the still small whisper at Horeb, and in the call of the Shepherd which His sheep infallibly know.
webster_full: VOICE, n. 1. Sound or audible noise uttered by the mouth, either of human beings or of other animals.
2. Any sound made by the breath; as the voice of a trumpet, the voice of many waters. Rev. 1.
3. Language; words; expression of the mind; as, the voice of nature, the voice of conscience.
4. Vote; suffrage; opinion or choice expressed. Acts 26.
5. In Scripture, the voice of the LORD God walking in the garden. Gen. 3. A still small voice. 1 Kings 19. My sheep hear my voice. John 10.
corruption_summary: The voice of God is relocated from Scripture to the believer's impressions, so that inward promptings acquire the authority of revelation; while the opposite error denies that God has spoken personally at all.
corruption_paragraphs: The most widespread evangelical corruption of this word is the confident report of a private voice — God told me, God spoke to me — used of impressions, impulses, and strong desires, and carrying an authority no one may examine. The damage is twofold. It renders the speaker unaccountable, since an inward voice cannot be tested by anyone else; and it quietly demotes Scripture, which becomes one source of guidance among others rather than the voice of God itself. The dictionary is cessationist on principle and follows the closed canon: God who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son. The living voice of God to the church now is the voice that is written, which is why the Spirit's work is described as bringing to remembrance what Christ said rather than supplementing it.

The opposite corruption is the deist instinct, dressed in modern clothing: that God, if He exists, does not speak; that religious language is the human search for meaning rather than a response to address. Scripture's whole structure denies this. It opens with God speaking the world into being, records a voice in a garden, a voice at Sinai that the people begged would stop, a voice from a cloud at the transfiguration, and closes with a voice from the throne. The principle to recover is that Christianity is a religion of hearing before it is a religion of experience — faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God — and that a man's deepest problem is not that he cannot find God's voice but that, like Adam, he is hiding from it.
roots_summary: Hebrew qōl means voice or any sound — thunder, trumpet, tumult — and idiomatically to hearken to the voice is to obey. Greek phōnē is a voice, sound, or tone, and gives the English phonetic.
roots_lines: Hebrew qōl (H6963) — voice, sound, noise; used of speech, thunder, trumpets, and the rustle of leaves alike.
Hebrew shāma' b'qōl — to hear in the voice, the standard idiom for obey; because thou hast hearkened unto the voice of thy wife (Gen 3:17).
Hebrew qōl d'māmâh daqqâh — a still small voice, literally a sound of thin silence; the LORD's answer to Elijah at Horeb (1Ki 19:12).
Greek phōnē (G5456) — voice, sound, tone; my sheep hear my voice (Joh 10:27), and the voice of the archangel at the last trump.
Greek akouō (G191) — to hear, and in the Hebraic sense to heed; he that hath ears to hear, let him hear.
usage: Of the voice sinners hide from: they heard the voice of the LORD God walking in the garden (Gen 3:8).
Of the whisper rather than the spectacle: after the fire a still small voice (1Ki 19:12).
Of the sheep's recognition: my sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me (Joh 10:27).

etymology: From Old English gesiht, from the root of see. The Hebrew idiom is the key to the biblical usage: the ordinary phrase for in the sight of is b''ēnē, literally in the eyes of. To do a thing in God's sight is to do it in His eyes, and so the word carries not observation only but judgment — what a thing looks like to the One whose estimate is final.
biblical_def: Sight in Scripture means three things which run together: physical seeing, the divine estimate of a matter, and the mode of knowing that faith replaces. The Hebrew idiom governs the middle sense, and the whole history of the kings is written in it — each did that which was right, or evil, in the sight of the LORD. Grace itself is described in the same terms, and the sentence that turns the flood narrative is one of the shortest in Scripture: “But Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD” (Gen 6:8). What God's eyes make of a man is the only verdict that will stand, which is why the psalmist submits not only his words but the thoughts behind them to that court: “Let the words of my mouth, and the meditation of my heart, be acceptable in thy sight, O LORD, my strength, and my redeemer” (Psa 19:14). Physical sight is one of the great signs of the Messiah's coming, named in the text He read at Nazareth: He was sent “to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised” (Luk 4:18) — and He gave it repeatedly, to men born blind, as a parable of what He does for souls. Yet the Christian's present life is deliberately not conducted by sight, and Paul states the principle in a parenthesis that governs everything around it: “(For we walk by faith, not by sight:)” (2Co 5:7). Sight is promised, not withheld — now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face. It is postponed, and faith is the appointed way of walking until it comes.
webster_summary: The act or faculty of seeing; view or notice; the estimate or judgment of one who sees — whence the Hebrew idiom in the sight, that is, in the eyes, of the LORD; and the mode of knowing which faith replaces in this life.
webster_full: SIGHT, n. 1. The act of seeing; perception of objects by the eye; view.
2. The faculty of vision, or of perceiving objects by the instrumentality of the eyes.
3. Open view; a situation admitting of free view; as, the town lies in sight of the sea.
4. Estimation; judgment; opinion; as, in the sight of God. In Hebrew, in the eyes of.
5. In Scripture, Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD. Gen. 6. We walk by faith, not by sight. 2 Cor. 5.
corruption_summary: Faith is redefined as a leap taken against evidence, so that walking by faith is made to mean believing without grounds, when Scripture means acting on the testimony of God about things not yet visible.
corruption_paragraphs: 2Co 5:7 is regularly enlisted to defend a faith held in defiance of evidence — the notion that believing without reasons is the more spiritual act, and that asking for grounds is itself a failure of trust. That is not the contrast Paul draws. His antithesis is not between faith and evidence but between faith and sight: between resting on the testimony of God concerning what is real but not yet visible, and requiring that a thing be present to the eye before it is counted real. Scripture everywhere appeals to grounds. Luke writes so that Theophilus may know the certainty of those things; Peter insists they did not follow cunningly devised fables but were eyewitnesses; Paul lists the resurrection appearances by name and number and stakes the entire faith on whether Christ is risen. Faith in the Bible is a well-founded confidence in a God who has spoken and acted publicly, not a decision to believe without cause.

The mirror-image corruption demands sight now, and it appears wherever a believer's assurance is made to rest on what he can currently see — the visible success of a work, the felt presence of God, health, or prosperity. Scripture warns that this leaves a man at the mercy of his circumstances, and it holds up as its models men who died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off. The principle to recover is that the postponement of sight is temporary and purposeful: God is training a people to trust His word about what is not yet visible, and He will not withhold the sight forever. Blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed — a beatitude spoken to men who would themselves see.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'ayin is an eye, and b''ēnē is the idiom in the sight of; mar'eh is an appearance or vision. Greek opsis is appearance or countenance, eidos is that which is seen, and anablepsis is recovery of sight.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'ayin (H5869) — an eye; and by idiom the sight, judgment, or estimate of the one who sees; right in his own eyes (Jdg 21:25).
Hebrew mar'eh (H4758) — sight, appearance, vision; the look of a thing as distinct from what it is.
Greek eidos (G1491) — that which is seen, outward appearance; the word behind sight in 2Co 5:7, so faith is contrasted with mere appearance.
Greek anablepsis (G309) — recovery of sight; used in Luk 4:18 of the Messiah's promised work, from anablepō, to look up or see again.
Greek enōpion (G1799) — before, in the sight of; the Greek equivalent of the Hebrew idiom, as acceptable in thy sight.
usage: Of God's estimate as the decisive one: Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD (Gen 6:8).
Of submitting heart and speech to that estimate: acceptable in thy sight, O LORD, my strength, and my redeemer (Psa 19:14).
Of the present mode of the Christian life: we walk by faith, not by sight (2Co 5:7).

pos: n. and v. (rendering Hebrew 'ānâh, Greek apokrinomai and apologia)
etymology: From Old English andswaru, a swearing against — originally a sworn reply to a charge, which is why the word keeps a legal flavour in English. The Hebrew 'ānâh means to answer, respond, or testify, and its legal sense stands behind the ninth commandment's false witness. The Greek apologia is likewise a courtroom word — a defence spoken in reply to an accusation — and it is the word Peter uses of the Christian's duty to explain his hope.
biblical_def: Answer in Scripture is chiefly a question of manner, and the Bible's counsel on it is remarkably practical. Proverbs makes the tone of a reply a moral matter with visible consequences: “A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger” (Pro 15:1). The observation is not that softness is always effective, but that the reply itself is one of the two forces at work in every quarrel, and a man governs one of them. Paul makes the same point a rule of Christian speech and grounds it in preparation rather than instinct: “Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man” (Col 4:6) — grace and salt together, so that speech is neither insipid nor corrosive, and the every man forbids the common practice of reserving courtesy for those who deserve it. Peter turns the word to its formal sense and lays a standing obligation on every believer: “But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear” (1Pe 3:15). The requirements are exact — a settled reverence within, a reasoned account, constant readiness, and meekness in the delivery. There is also a time for no answer at all, and the Lord Jesus set the pattern before Pilate and the chief priests: “And when he was accused of the chief priests and elders, he answered nothing” (Mat 27:12). Silence before a court that has already decided is not weakness; it is a form of testimony.
webster_summary: A reply to a question, charge, or objection; a defence or account given in reply; and in Scripture the soft answer that turns away wrath, the gracious answer seasoned with salt, and the reasoned answer every believer must be ready to give for his hope.
webster_full: ANSWER, v. 1. To speak in return to a call or question, or to a speech, declaration or argument.
2. To be accountable, liable or responsible; as, to answer for another's debt.
3. To be equivalent to; to correspond with; as, one thing answers to another.
4. n. A reply; that which is said in return to a question or objection. A soft answer turneth away wrath. Prov. 15.
5. A defence; an account or vindication given in reply, as before a tribunal. Be ready always to give an answer. 1 Pet. 3.
corruption_summary: The command to give an answer is treated as optional for ordinary believers and left to specialists, while the manner Scripture attaches to it — meekness and fear — is discarded wherever the argument is thought to be winning.
corruption_paragraphs: 1Pe 3:15 is addressed to a whole persecuted church, not to a class of trained defenders, and the duty it lays down is universal: be ready always, to every man that asketh. Where this is treated as the province of specialists, two things follow. Ordinary Christians conclude that they need not be able to say why they believe, and their faith becomes inarticulate to themselves as well as to others; and the church's witness contracts to the few occasions when an expert is present. Peter assumes the opposite: that believers living visibly different lives under pressure will be asked, and that the question deserves a reason. The command begins inwardly — sanctify the Lord God in your hearts — because a man who has settled who is Lord within has something to say when the question comes.

The second corruption concerns manner, and it is now the more common failure. The same verse that requires an answer prescribes its temper: with meekness and fear. Contemporary argument, including Christian argument, is conducted largely for the benefit of onlookers who already agree, and rewards the reply that humiliates. Scripture's standard makes that a disqualification rather than a victory, since the servant of the Lord must not strive, but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient, in meekness instructing those that oppose themselves. The principle to recover joins the two halves: an answer that is reasoned but contemptuous has failed the command as surely as no answer at all, and a soft answer is not a weak one — it is the reply that turns away wrath (Pro 15:1) rather than feeding it.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'ānâh is to answer, respond, or testify, with a legal sense of replying to a charge. Greek apokrinomai is to reply, and apologia is a formal defence spoken before a tribunal, whence the English apologetics.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'ānâh (H6030) — to answer, respond, testify; used of replying to a question and of bearing witness in a cause.
Hebrew ma'aneh (H4617) — an answer or reply; a soft answer turneth away wrath (Pro 15:1), literally an answer of gentleness.
Greek apokrinomai (G611) — to answer or reply; the ordinary narrative verb, as Jesus answered and said unto them.
Greek apologia (G627) — a verbal defence, a reasoned reply to an accusation; the word in 1Pe 3:15 and in Paul's defence before Agrippa.
Greek eperotēma (G1906) — an enquiry or appeal; the answer of a good conscience toward God (1Pe 3:21), a different sense of the English word.
usage: Of the manner of reply: a soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger (Pro 15:1).
Of prepared and gracious speech: let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt (Col 4:6).
Of the standing duty to explain the hope: be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you (1Pe 3:15).

pos: n. and v. (rendering Hebrew ts'āqâh and sh''âh, Greek krazō and boaō)
etymology: From Old French crier, from Latin quiritare, to wail or call for help — said to derive from calling upon the Quirites, the citizens, for aid. The Hebrew ts'āqâh is a shriek or outcry wrung out by distress rather than a considered petition, and the Greek krazō is likewise a raw, loud call. Scripture's point is that this — not eloquence — is what God undertakes to hear.
biblical_def: A cry in Scripture is prayer stripped of composure, and it is the form of prayer God is most often said to hear. The Exodus begins with one, and the divine response is described in a sequence of verbs that leaves nothing to chance: “I have surely seen the affliction of my people which are in Egypt, and have heard their cry by reason of their taskmasters; for I know their sorrows” (Exo 3:7). God sees, hears, and knows — and then comes down. The psalms make the same connection a settled rule of God's dealings: “The righteous cry, and the LORD heareth, and delivereth them out of all their troubles” (Psa 34:17). Hearing is not always the same as answering at once, and David records a wait without complaining of it: “I waited patiently for the LORD; and he inclined unto me, and heard my cry” (Psa 40:1) — the inclining being the picture of One who bends down to catch what is said. The New Testament traces the cry to its source in the believer and finds the Spirit there, so that the rawest prayer is also the most evidently supernatural: “For ye have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear; but ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father” (Rom 8:15). The word for slaves crying under taskmasters becomes the word for sons crying to a Father. And Scripture records that the cry of the oppressed rises whether or not anyone means it as prayer: the blood of Abel cried from the ground, and the hire of the defrauded labourer cries in the ears of the Lord of sabaoth.
webster_summary: To call loudly, especially in distress; an outcry, clamour, or lamentation; and in Scripture the cry of the oppressed which God hears and answers, and the cry of Abba, Father, which the Spirit of adoption prompts in His children.
webster_full: CRY, v. 1. To utter a loud voice; to speak, call or exclaim with vehemence.
2. To call importunately; to utter a loud voice with earnestness, by way of prayer or entreaty.
3. To utter a loud voice in weeping; to lament aloud.
4. n. A loud utterance; especially, the utterance of a sudden or violent emotion; an outcry.
5. In Scripture, the cry of the oppressed, which God regards. Exod. 3. The righteous cry, and the LORD heareth. Psalm 34.
corruption_summary: Prayer is reduced to composed and articulate performance, so that the raw cry of grief is treated as immature; and the cry of the oppressed is either ignored by the comfortable or annexed to political frameworks Scripture does not use.
corruption_paragraphs: Where prayer is judged by fluency, the cry disappears. A congregation trained to admire well-turned petitions learns that grief must be composed before it can be brought, and the psalms — a third of which are laments, some of them ending without resolution — become unusable. Scripture's pattern is the opposite. It preserves prayers that shriek: how long, O LORD? my God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? out of the depths have I cried unto thee. The Lord Jesus Himself, in the days of his flesh, offered up prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears. A theology that cannot make room for that has made prayer a performance rather than the voice of a child, and has quietly excluded the suffering at the moment they most need to speak.

The cry of the oppressed suffers a double corruption. The comfortable dismiss it, forgetting that Scripture treats such cries as entering God's ears whether or not the crier is pious — the wages of the defrauded reaper cry, and the LORD hears them. But it is equally a corruption to annex those cries to frameworks that replace Scripture's categories with an oppressor-oppressed binary determined by group identity, so that guilt and innocence are read off membership rather than off conduct before God. The Bible's categories are concrete and personal: the widow, the fatherless, the stranger, the hired servant defrauded of his wages, the poor man whose cloak is kept overnight. The principle to recover is that God hears actual cries from actual sufferers and requires actual justice — ye shall not respect persons in judgment, neither the person of the poor nor the person of the mighty.
roots_summary: Hebrew ts'āqâh is an outcry wrung out by distress; sh''âh is a cry for help; rinnâh is a ringing cry, whether of joy or entreaty. Greek krazō is to cry out with a loud, raw voice, and boaō is to call aloud.
roots_lines: Hebrew ts'āqâh (H6818) — an outcry, shriek of distress; the cry of Israel under the taskmasters (Exo 3:7) and the cry of Sodom.
Hebrew sh''âh (H7775) — a cry for help, entreaty; let my cry come unto thee (Psa 102:1).
Hebrew rinnâh (H7440) — a ringing or resounding cry; used of both jubilation and supplication, as attend unto my cry (Psa 17:1).
Greek krazō (G2896) — to croak, shriek, or cry out; whereby we cry, Abba, Father (Rom 8:15), and the cry of the blind man Christ stopped for.
Greek boaō (G994) — to call or shout aloud; the voice of one crying in the wilderness (Mat 3:3).
usage: Of the cry God hears and acts upon: I have heard their cry by reason of their taskmasters; for I know their sorrows (Exo 3:7).
Of the rule of God's dealings: the righteous cry, and the LORD heareth, and delivereth them (Psa 34:17).
Of the Spirit's cry in the believer: the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father (Rom 8:15).

etymology: From Latin causa, a reason, and also a lawsuit — the two senses that English still carries. The Hebrew rīb is squarely the legal one: it means a dispute, controversy, or suit, and the verb means to contend at law. This is why Scripture speaks of God pleading a man's cause: the picture is not of sympathy but of an advocate rising in court to argue a case that belongs to somebody else.
biblical_def: Cause in Scripture is a legal word, and the doctrine it carries is that the believer's case is argued by Another. David does not ask God to feel for him but to appear for him: “Judge me, O God, and plead my cause against an ungodly nation: O deliver me from the deceitful and unjust man” (Psa 43:1). Job, who has no advocate among his friends, resolves on the same course: “I would seek unto God, and unto God would I commit my cause” (Job 5:8) — committing a cause being the act of handing a suit over to someone who will conduct it. The obligation runs downward as well, and Scripture assigns to the powerful the duty of arguing for those who cannot argue for themselves: “Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction” (Pro 31:8). This is addressed to a king, and it is one of the plainest statements in the Bible of what authority is for. The word then takes its darkest turn in the Lord's account of His own trial, where He applies the psalm to Himself and names the exact charge: “this cometh to pass, that the word might be fulfilled that is written in their law, They hated me without a cause” (Joh 15:25). The hatred had no case behind it — there was no rīb, no ground of suit — and He tells His disciples so in order that they may know what to expect when the same causeless hatred falls on them.
webster_summary: That which produces an effect; a reason or ground; and in the legal sense a suit, controversy, or case to be pleaded — whence God pleading the cause of His people, the duty of pleading for the helpless, and Christ hated without a cause.
webster_full: CAUSE, n. 1. A suit or action in court; any legal process which a party institutes to obtain his demand.
2. That which produces an effect; that which impels into existence, or by its agency or operation produces what did not before exist.
3. The reason or motive that urges, moves, or impels the mind to act or omit action.
4. Sake; account; as, for my cause; for thy cause.
5. In Scripture, plead my cause. Psalm 43. Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction. Prov. 31.
corruption_summary: Advocacy is detached from truth and made a matter of loyalty to a side, so that pleading a cause means arguing for one's own party rather than for what is just — and Scripture's command to plead for the helpless is either politicised or ignored.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture's law of causes contains a command that no partisan age finds tolerable: thou shalt not countenance a poor man in his cause, set alongside its opposite, thou shalt not wrest the judgment of thy poor. Both are given, and together they forbid deciding a case by the identity of the parties in either direction. Justice in the Bible is blind to persons and sighted toward facts: ye shall not respect persons in judgment; but ye shall hear the small as well as the great. Where advocacy is reduced to loyalty — where a man's cause is judged by which side he is on — the courts, the press, and eventually the churches lose the capacity to correct their own. The corruption is not that people take sides but that taking a side has replaced weighing a case.

The command of Pro 31:8 is corrupted in the opposite direction by neglect. It is spoken to a king by his mother, and it makes the defence of those with no voice a duty of office rather than an optional charity — such as are appointed to destruction being those already marked for death, whose case nobody will take. Applied honestly, it reaches the unborn, the condemned, the friendless accused, and the aged whose lives are quietly reckoned burdensome. The principle to recover joins both halves of the biblical law: the believer pleads for the voiceless because God commands it, and pleads truthfully because the God who commands it will not accept a lie told in a good cause — and he does so knowing that his own cause is committed to One who was Himself hated without a cause (Joh 15:25).
roots_summary: Hebrew rīb is a legal dispute, controversy, or suit, and the verb is to contend at law; dābār is a word, and hence a matter or case. Greek aitia is a cause, ground, or accusation, and dōrean is the adverb without a cause, gratuitously.
roots_lines: Hebrew rīb (H7379) — a controversy, suit, or legal contention; plead my cause (Psa 43:1), and the LORD's controversy with His people (Mic 6:2).
Hebrew dābār (H1697) — a word, and hence a matter, affair, or case brought for judgment; the hard causes brought to Moses (Exo 18:26).
Hebrew dīn (H1779) — judgment or a legal cause; he judged the cause of the poor and needy (Jer 22:16).
Greek aitia (G156) — cause, ground, accusation; Pilate's verdict, I find no fault (no aitia) in this man (Luk 23:4).
Greek dōrean (G1432) — freely, gratuitously, without cause; they hated me without a cause (Joh 15:25), the same word rendered freely of justification in Rom 3:24.
usage: Of God as advocate: judge me, O God, and plead my cause against an ungodly nation (Psa 43:1).
Of committing one's case to God: unto God would I commit my cause (Job 5:8).
Of pleading for the voiceless: open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction (Pro 31:8).

etymology: From Old French maniere, from Latin manuarius, of the hand — the way a thing is handled. The biblical words are heavier than the English suggests. Hebrew mishpāt is judgment or ordinance, and when it is rendered manner it means the prescribed way a thing is to be done; derek is a road, and hence a settled way of life. Greek anastrophē, which the King James renders conversation, means one's whole turning-about in the world — conduct as a habit rather than as an act.
biblical_def: Manner in Scripture means settled habit, the way a man customarily goes, and it is treated as the true index of what he is. Paul can appeal to it as evidence before a court: “My manner of life from my youth, which was at the first among mine own nation at Jerusalem, know all the Jews” (Act 26:4) — a life whose pattern was public and could be examined. Habit works in both directions, and Hebrews names a bad one without softening it: “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching” (Heb 10:25). The neglect described is not a decision but a drift — a manner, something that has become customary — and the remedy prescribed is not merely resolve but the counter-habit of mutual exhortation. The standard set over all Christian habit is the character of God Himself, and it admits of no compartments: “But as he which hath called you is holy, so be ye holy in all manner of conversation” (1Pe 1:15). All manner forbids the arrangement by which a man is devout in one sphere and unreformed in another. The word also names the surprise of the disciples at the character of Christ — what manner of man is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him? — and the wonder of John at the Father's love: behold, what manner of love the Father hath bestowed upon us.
webster_summary: The way in which a thing is done; a settled habit or custom; and in Scripture the manner of life which is a man's public pattern, the manner of some who forsake the assembly, and the holiness required in all manner of conversation.
webster_full: MANNER, n. 1. Form; method; way of performing or executing.
2. Custom; habitual practice; as, this was the manner of the ancients.
3. Sort; kind; as all manner of men, all manner of evil. Matt. 5.
4. Certain degree or measure; as, it is in a manner done.
5. In Scripture, the manner of life; conversation or habitual conduct. Be ye holy in all manner of conversation. 1 Pet. 1.
corruption_summary: Christian obedience is reduced to intentions and moments of decision, so that settled habit — which Scripture treats as the real measure of a man — is dismissed as mere externals or legalism.
corruption_paragraphs: A religion of decisive moments without settled habits is not the Christianity of the New Testament. Scripture consistently examines the manner: Paul appeals to a life whose pattern from youth was open to inspection; the qualifications for elders are almost entirely a description of habits rather than gifts; and the writer to the Hebrews diagnoses a spiritual condition by noting what had become customary. Where habit is dismissed as externalism, two errors follow. Sanctification is expected to arrive by crisis rather than by the ordinary means God appointed, and the person who keeps failing concludes he lacks sincerity when in fact he lacks practice. Scripture's remedy is unglamorous and corporate: assembling, exhorting, and the more so as the day approaches.

The opposite corruption inflates manner into everything, so that conformity of behaviour is mistaken for the new birth. The Pharisees kept a manner of life that Paul could describe as touching the righteousness which is in the law, blameless, and it did not save him; he counted it loss for Christ. Scripture always drives the question inward — make the tree good, and his fruit good — while refusing to let the inward stand alone, since by their fruits ye shall know them. The principle to recover holds both: habit is the evidence of the heart and not a substitute for it, and the command be ye holy in all manner of conversation (1Pe 1:15) reaches the whole of a man's customary life precisely because it is aimed at the whole of his heart.
roots_summary: Hebrew mishpāt is judgment, ordinance, or the prescribed manner of a thing; derek is a way or road, hence a course of life. Greek tropos is a manner or fashion, and anastrophē is conduct or manner of life, rendered conversation in the King James.
roots_lines: Hebrew mishpāt (H4941) — judgment, ordinance, prescribed manner; the manner of the king (1Sa 8:9) is his settled ordinance of rule.
Hebrew derek (H1870) — a way, road, journey; and hence a settled course or manner of life, as the way of the ungodly shall perish (Psa 1:6).
Greek tropos (G5158) — a turn, manner, fashion; how often would I have gathered thy children, even as a hen gathereth (Mat 23:37).
Greek anastrophē (G391) — conduct, behaviour, manner of life; rendered conversation throughout the King James, as in 1Pe 1:15.
Greek ethos (G1485) — custom or habit; as his custom was, he went into the synagogue on the sabbath day (Luk 4:16).
usage: Of a public and examinable pattern: my manner of life from my youth... know all the Jews (Act 26:4).
Of a bad habit named: not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is (Heb 10:25).
Of the scope of holiness: be ye holy in all manner of conversation (1Pe 1:15).
scriptures: Acts 26:4
My manner of life from my youth, which was at the first among mine own nation at Jerusalem, know all the Jews;
Hebrews 10:25
Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.
1 Peter 1:15
But as he which hath called you is holy, so be ye holy in all manner of conversation;
Matthew 5:11
Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake .

etymology: From Old English thing, which meant an assembly or a matter brought before one — the Icelandic parliament is still the Althing. The English word therefore began as a word for a case under discussion and only later became the vaguest noun in the language. Hebrew dābār travels the same road in reverse: it means a word, and because a word spoken by God becomes an event, it also means a thing or matter. In Hebrew, word and deed are one noun.
biblical_def: Thing is the plainest word in the language, and Scripture uses it at the highest moments, where the question is what God is able to do. The pattern statement is put as a question to Abraham after Sarah laughs, and it is left hanging so that she must answer it: “Is any thing too hard for the LORD? At the time appointed I will return unto thee, according to the time of life, and Sarah shall have a son” (Gen 18:14). The same question is put back to God by Jeremiah, in a prayer, as a confession rather than an enquiry, and God repeats it to him: “Behold, I am the LORD, the God of all flesh: is there any thing too hard for me?” (Jer 32:27) — spoken while the Babylonians were besieging the city and the prophet had just been told to buy a field in it. Gabriel brings the same doctrine to Mary in its most compressed form: “For with God nothing shall be impossible” (Luk 1:37). Three impossibilities — a barren womb, a doomed nation, a virgin conception — and one answer given each time. The word also serves for the summing up of all human duty, where Ecclesiastes gathers a whole book of restless enquiry into a single sentence: “Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter: Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man” (Ecc 12:13). And the Lord Jesus reduces the crowded life of Martha to the same simplicity — one thing is needful.
webster_summary: Whatever exists or may be thought of; a matter, affair, or circumstance; and in Scripture the question is any thing too hard for the LORD, the one thing needful, and the whole matter of man's duty summed in fearing God and keeping His commandments.
webster_full: THING, n. 1. An event or action; that which is done or which comes to pass; as, we hear of strange things.
2. Any substance; that which is created; any particular article or commodity.
3. A matter or affair under consideration; as, this thing shall not be done.
4. Used of persons in contempt or in pity; as, poor thing.
5. In Scripture, is any thing too hard for the LORD? Gen. 18. One thing is needful. Luke 10. The conclusion of the whole matter. Eccl. 12.
corruption_summary: The promise that nothing is impossible with God is detached from God's revealed purpose and turned into a warrant for whatever the believer wants, so that omnipotence is made to serve human ambition.
corruption_paragraphs: “Nothing shall be impossible” is among the most abused sentences in Scripture. Lifted out of Luk 1:37, it becomes a general guarantee that any desire held with sufficient faith must be granted, and it is preached in exactly that form wherever the prosperity teachers are heard. Its setting forbids the use. It is spoken by an angel to a young woman who has just been told something she did not ask for, would not have chosen, and which would cost her reputation and very nearly her betrothal — and her reply is not a claim but a submission: be it unto me according to thy word. The same is true of the other two occurrences. Sarah is told what God has appointed, not what she has requested; Jeremiah is told to buy a field in a city God has determined to give to Babylon. In every case the divine omnipotence is attached to a divine purpose, and the comfort of the doctrine lies precisely there: what God has promised, nothing can prevent.

The opposite corruption is practical rather than doctrinal, and it is the commoner sin among the orthodox: to confess that nothing is too hard for the LORD while praying and living as though a good many things were. Sarah laughed within herself, and the narrative does not treat this as a small thing — God asks why she laughed, and the question is not answered. Jeremiah, having confessed in prayer that there is nothing too hard for God, is immediately asked whether he believes it about the field he has just bought. The principle to recover is that this doctrine is meant to be applied to particulars: to a specific dead marriage, a specific hardened child, a specific besetting sin. Fear God, and keep his commandments (Ecc 12:13) is the whole duty; and the God so feared is the God for whom nothing is too hard.
roots_summary: Hebrew dābār means both word and thing, since a word from God becomes an event; it is also the ordinary term for a matter or case. Greek pragma is a deed or matter, and rēma is a spoken word which, like the Hebrew, can mean the thing said.
roots_lines: Hebrew dābār (H1697) — word, matter, thing; the same noun for what is spoken and for what comes to pass, since God's word is His act.
Hebrew pālā' (H6381) — to be wonderful, extraordinary, too hard; the verb in is any thing too hard for the LORD (Gen 18:14).
Greek pragma (G4229) — a deed, matter, or thing done; the substance of things hoped for (Heb 11:1).
Greek rēma (G4487) — a spoken word, and by the Hebrew idiom the thing spoken of; the word behind nothing in Luk 1:37, literally no rēma shall be impossible.
Greek adunateō (G101) — to be without power, impossible; with God nothing shall be impossible (Luk 1:37).
usage: Of the question put to unbelief: is any thing too hard for the LORD? (Gen 18:14; Jer 32:27).
Of the annunciation: for with God nothing shall be impossible (Luk 1:37).
Of the summing up of duty: fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man (Ecc 12:13).
scriptures: Genesis 18:14
Is any thing too hard for the LORD? At the time appointed I will return unto thee, according to the time of life, and Sarah shall have a son.
Jeremiah 32:27
Behold, I am the LORD, the God of all flesh: is there any thing too hard for me?
Luke 1:37
For with God nothing shall be impossible.
Ecclesiastes 12:13
Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter: Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man.

etymology: From Old English sacu, a lawsuit, contention, or cause — the same root that gives German Sache, a matter or case. To do a thing for someone's sake was therefore, originally, to do it on his behalf as one would argue his case. The Hebrew l'ma'an means for the purpose of or on account of, and Scripture's most weighty uses of the phrase concern God acting for the sake of His own name.
biblical_def: Sake is the word by which Scripture states the reason a thing is done, and its most important use answers the question why God saves. The shepherd psalm does not ground the leading in the sheep's merit: “He restoreth my soul: he leadeth me in the paths of righteousness for his name's sake” (Psa 23:3). The motive is God's own name — His revealed character and reputation — and this is the strongest possible ground of assurance, since a salvation resting on the believer's worth could be lost with it, while one resting on God's name is as secure as God's regard for Himself. Ezekiel puts it bluntly: I do not this for your sakes, O house of Israel, but for mine holy name's sake. The second great use turns the word toward suffering, and the Lord Jesus makes His own name the ground of the last beatitude: “Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake” (Mat 5:11). The qualification is exact — falsely, and for my sake — which excludes suffering brought on by one's own folly or rudeness. Paul takes up an old psalm to describe the ordinary condition of the church: “For thy sake we are killed all the day long; we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter” (Rom 8:36); and he explains what such a life is for: “For we which live are alway delivered unto death for Jesus' sake, that the life also of Jesus might be made manifest in our mortal flesh” (2Co 4:11). The dying of the servant is the means by which the life of the Master becomes visible.
webster_summary: Final cause; end; purpose; account — the reason for which a thing is done; and in Scripture the name's sake for which God saves and leads, and the Christ's sake for which His people are reviled and delivered unto death.
webster_full: SAKE, n. 1. Final cause; end; purpose; or rather the purpose of obtaining. We say, a man labors for the sake of gain.
2. Account; regard to any person or thing. I will not again curse the ground any more for man's sake. Gen. 8.
3. Cause; reason; as, for the sake of peace, he yielded the point.
4. In the older sense, a cause or suit at law; contention; whence the phrase for one's sake, on his behalf.
5. In Scripture, he leadeth me in the paths of righteousness for his name's sake. Psalm 23. Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you for my sake. Matt. 5.
corruption_summary: Persecution language is claimed for consequences a believer has brought on himself by rudeness, folly, or partisanship, so that the beatitude's two conditions — falsely, and for Christ's sake — are quietly dropped.
corruption_paragraphs: The beatitude of Mat 5:11 is guarded by two qualifications, and both are routinely omitted. The first is falsely: the evil said must be untrue. A Christian who is disliked for being abrasive, dishonest, or careless in his dealings is not suffering reproach for righteousness; he is bearing the ordinary fruit of his conduct, and Peter says as much — let none of you suffer as a murderer, or as a thief, or as an evildoer, or as a busybody in other men's matters. The second qualification is for my sake. Opposition incurred for a political allegiance, a cultural preference, or a personal cause is not persecution for Christ, however sincerely the two are conflated. Where the qualifications are dropped, a genuine comfort becomes an instrument of self-deception, and the church loses the ability to tell a martyr from a nuisance.

There is a corresponding failure in the other direction: a squeamishness that will not admit persecution is normal Christian experience. Rom 8:36 quotes a psalm to describe not an extremity but the settled condition of God's people — killed all the day long, accounted as sheep for the slaughter — and Paul places it inside the chapter that begins with no condemnation and ends with no separation. He does not treat it as a contradiction of God's love but as one of the things that cannot separate us from it. The principle to recover is the purpose stated in 2Co 4:11: the believer is delivered unto death for Jesus' sake that the life also of Jesus might be made manifest. Suffering rightly borne is not merely endured; it is the appointed means by which a watching world sees the life of the risen Christ in mortal flesh.
roots_summary: Hebrew l'ma'an means for the sake of, on account of, to the end that; ba''ābūr means for the sake of or because of. Greek heneka is on account of, and dia with the accusative means because of or for the sake of.
roots_lines: Hebrew l'ma'an (H4616) — for the sake of, to the intent that; for his name's sake (Psa 23:3) and for thy servants' sake.
Hebrew ba''ābūr (H5668) — on account of, for the sake of; I will not again curse the ground for man's sake (Gen 8:21).
Hebrew shēm (H8034) — name; God's name being His revealed character, for His name's sake means according to who He has declared Himself to be.
Greek heneka (G1752) — on account of, for the sake of; blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake (Mat 5:10).
Greek dia (G1223) — through, and with the accusative, because of; delivered unto death for Jesus' sake (2Co 4:11).
usage: Of the ground of God's dealings: he leadeth me in the paths of righteousness for his name's sake (Psa 23:3).
Of the qualified beatitude: when men shall revile you... falsely, for my sake (Mat 5:11).
Of the purpose of the believer's suffering: delivered unto death for Jesus' sake, that the life also of Jesus might be made manifest (2Co 4:11).
scriptures: Psalm 23:3
He restoreth my soul: he leadeth me in the paths of righteousness for his name's sake.
Matthew 5:11
Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake .
Romans 8:36
As it is written, For thy sake we are killed all the day long; we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter.
2 Corinthians 4:11
For we which live are alway delivered unto death for Jesus' sake, that the life also of Jesus might be made manifest in our mortal flesh.

etymology: From Latin pars, a portion or share. The Hebrew chēleq means a portion or allotment — specifically one's share in the division of the land — and it is the word behind the great confession that the LORD Himself is the believer's portion. To ask what a man's part is, in the Hebrew sense, is to ask what he was allotted when the inheritance was divided.
biblical_def: Part in Scripture is a word about portions, and it asks two questions: what has been allotted to a man, and how much of him has been given to God. God's claim runs to the innermost portion, where no observer can follow: “Behold, thou desirest truth in the inward parts: and in the hidden part thou shalt make me to know wisdom” (Psa 51:6) — David's confession locating the demand not at the level of conduct but of the hidden man of the heart. The Lord Jesus uses the word to settle the dispute in a kitchen at Bethany, and His verdict is one of the tenderest in the Gospels: “But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luk 10:42). Martha's service was not condemned; it was ranked. Mary had chosen a portion with a quality no other has — it cannot be confiscated. Against this stands the terrible sentence on Simon the sorcerer, who wished to buy the gift of God and was told where he stood: “Thou hast neither part nor lot in this matter: for thy heart is not right in the sight of God” (Act 8:21) — a man may be baptised, continue with the apostles, and still have no portion. And the word governs the honest limits of present knowledge: “For we know in part, and we prophesy in part” (1Co 13:9). What we have of God now is genuine and partial at once, which is why charity outlasts knowledge and why the man who claims a complete system has mistaken his portion for the whole estate.
webster_summary: A portion, piece, or share of a whole; the allotment assigned to one; and in Scripture the inward parts where God requires truth, the good part Mary chose which cannot be taken away, and the knowledge we have only in part.
webster_full: PART, n. 1. A portion, piece or fragment separated from a whole thing.
2. A portion or share; as, he has his part of the inheritance.
3. Something relating or belonging to; that which concerns; as, for my part.
4. Side; party; interest; as, he took part with the weaker side.
5. In Scripture, an allotted portion. The LORD is my portion. Lam. 3. Mary hath chosen that good part. Luke 10. We know in part. 1 Cor. 13.
corruption_summary: Partial knowledge is treated as no knowledge at all, so that the honest limits of 1 Corinthians 13:9 are made to underwrite a general doctrinal agnosticism in which nothing may be affirmed with confidence.
corruption_paragraphs: “We know in part” is now regularly deployed to suspend judgment on doctrines Scripture states plainly — as though the partiality of present knowledge rendered all conviction premature and every confession provisional. Paul's own practice refutes the use. The same apostle who wrote that we know in part also wrote that if any man preach any other gospel, let him be accursed, and delivered as of first importance a list of facts he expected to be believed without hesitation. Partial is not the same as uncertain. A man who sees a landscape through a window sees genuinely, though not wholly, and what he sees he may report with confidence. The chapter's point is not that doctrine is unreliable but that knowledge without charity is nothing, and that the gifts by which we now know will cease when the perfect is come — while charity never faileth.

The opposite corruption forgets the in part altogether and builds systems that claim to have accounted for everything, treating secret things as though they had been revealed. Deuteronomy draws the line: the secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children. Where that line is crossed, speculation hardens into a test of orthodoxy and the church divides over what God did not disclose. The principle to recover is that Scripture gives certainty and reticence together — certainty about what God has spoken, reticence about what He has not — and that the good part Mary chose (Luk 10:42) was not a complete comprehension of Christ but a settled place at His feet, hearing His word.
roots_summary: Hebrew chēleq is a portion, share, or allotment, especially in the division of land; tūchah is the inward part. Greek meros is a part, share, or portion, and klerus is a lot or inheritance, whence part nor lot.
roots_lines: Hebrew chēleq (H2506) — portion, share, allotment; the LORD is the portion of mine inheritance (Psa 16:5), and Levi's portion is the LORD Himself.
Hebrew tūchah (H2910) — the inward parts, the innermost being; thou desirest truth in the inward parts (Psa 51:6).
Greek meros (G3313) — a part, share, portion; we know in part (1Co 13:9), and thou hast no part with me (Joh 13:8).
Greek klēros (G2819) — a lot, and hence an inheritance assigned by lot; neither part nor lot in this matter (Act 8:21).
Greek meris (G3310) — a portion or share; Mary hath chosen that good part (Luk 10:42), the word implying a deliberate allotment.
usage: Of God's claim on the innermost portion: thou desirest truth in the inward parts (Psa 51:6).
Of the portion that cannot be confiscated: Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her (Luk 10:42).
Of the limits of present knowledge: we know in part, and we prophesy in part (1Co 13:9).

Behold, thou desirest truth in the inward parts: and in the hidden part thou shalt make me to know wisdom.
Luke 10:42

Acts 8:21
Thou hast neither part nor lot in this matter: for thy heart is not right in the sight of God.
1 Corinthians 13:9
For we know in part, and we prophesy in part.

etymology: From Old English ende. The two biblical words divide the sense usefully. Hebrew qēts is a cut-off point, a termination; 'acharīth is the latter end, the outcome of a thing, what it comes to. Greek telos carries both termination and goal — the end of a road being also the purpose of walking it — which is why telos gives English teleology. Scripture's doctrine of the end is almost always this second sense: not merely when a thing stops but what it was for.
biblical_def: End in Scripture means outcome and goal more often than mere termination, and the distinction carries most of the doctrine. Ecclesiastes states the principle as a proverb of judgment: “Better is the end of a thing than the beginning thereof: and the patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit” (Ecc 7:8) — beginnings are cheap and impressive, and only the end shows what a thing was. The Lord Jesus applies this to profession of faith in words that have troubled every shallow assurance: “But he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved” (Mat 24:13). The verse does not teach that endurance earns salvation; it teaches that endurance is what saving faith does, so that perseverance is the evidence rather than the price. Paul then uses the word in its highest sense, making Christ the goal toward which the whole law was always pointing: “For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth” (Rom 10:4). Telos here means terminus and purpose together — the law's demands are ended for the believer because they are fulfilled in Christ, and the law's whole design is reached in Him. Peter draws the practical conclusion for a church under pressure, and it is notably sober rather than feverish: “But the end of all things is at hand: be ye therefore sober, and watch unto prayer” (1Pe 4:7). Scripture's expectation of the end never produces excitement or withdrawal; it produces sobriety, watchfulness, and prayer.
webster_summary: The extreme point or termination of a thing; the conclusion or issue; the final purpose or design for which a thing exists; and in Scripture the end one must endure unto, and Christ who is the end of the law for righteousness.
webster_full: END, n. 1. The extreme point of a line, or of any thing that has more length than breadth.
2. The last; the conclusion; the close; termination; as the end of the year.
3. Final determination; issue; result; the latter end, or what a thing comes to at last.
4. Ultimate object or purpose; final cause; that for the sake of which a thing is done. The end of the commandment is charity. 1 Tim. 1.
5. In Scripture, he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved. Matt. 24. Christ is the end of the law. Rom. 10.
corruption_summary: Perseverance is either turned into a condition the believer must meet in his own strength, robbing assurance, or dissolved altogether into a bare once-saved formula which needs no fruit — and the end of all things is made a subject for speculation rather than sobriety.
corruption_paragraphs: Mat 24:13 is pulled in two wrong directions. On one side it is read as making salvation conditional upon a stamina the believer must supply, so that assurance becomes impossible and the Christian life is lived under audit. On the other it is emptied by a bare formula which holds that a past decision guarantees a future regardless of any fruit whatever, so that endurance is optional and apostasy proves nothing. The Reformed doctrine avoids both by naming the agent: the perseverance of the saints is grounded in the preservation of God. He which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ; my sheep shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand. Endurance is therefore certain because God keeps His people, and it is genuinely necessary because it is the way He keeps them — the evidence of regeneration rather than its price, and not a bare formula that can be recited over a life with no fruit at all.

The second corruption concerns the end of all things. Peter's statement that it is at hand is made the occasion for date-setting, chart-making, and a fascination with the sequence of last events that Scripture nowhere encourages — and, at the other extreme, for a withdrawal from ordinary duty on the ground that the world is ending anyway. Peter's own inference is neither: be ye therefore sober, and watch unto prayer, and in the next verse, above all things have fervent charity among yourselves. The dictionary holds the closed canon and the certain return of Christ while declining the novelties of a nineteenth-century prophetic system. The principle to recover is that the nearness of the end is given as a motive to sobriety, prayer, and love — and that a man ready to meet Christ today needs no calendar.
roots_summary: Hebrew qēts is a cut-off point or termination; 'acharīth is the latter end, the outcome or what a thing comes to. Greek telos means both termination and goal, and sunteleia is the consummation of an age.
roots_lines: Hebrew qēts (H7093) — an end, cut-off point, or limit; from a root meaning to cut off, as the end of days.
Hebrew 'acharīth (H319) — the latter end, outcome, or issue of a thing; oh that they would consider their latter end (Deu 32:29).
Greek telos (G5056) — end, termination, and also goal or purpose; Christ is the end of the law (Rom 10:4), both its terminus and its aim.
Greek sunteleia (G4930) — a completing together, consummation; the end of the world (Mat 28:20), literally the consummation of the age.
Greek hupomenō (G5278) — to remain under, endure, persevere; he that shall endure unto the end (Mat 24:13).
usage: Of the end as the test of a thing: better is the end of a thing than the beginning thereof (Ecc 7:8).
Of Christ as the law's goal: Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth (Rom 10:4).
Of the sobriety the end requires: the end of all things is at hand: be ye therefore sober, and watch unto prayer (1Pe 4:7).

Better is the end of a thing than the beginning thereof: and the patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit.
Matthew 24:13
But he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved.
Romans 10:4
For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth.

But the end of all things is at hand: be ye therefore sober, and watch unto prayer.
